transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I just can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. Like, I’ve got patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines, team decisions—well, the gallery thing is kind of a side project, but it has real deadlines—and I’ll sit down intending to tackle the important thing, and somehow I end up doing whatever is loudest or most urgent-feeling instead.

It’s not that I don’t care or don’t understand what needs doing. It’s more like I can’t get the pieces lined up in the right order, and then I’m reacting all day instead of actually moving things forward.
When you were a child, did you often have the same kind of trouble getting organized and following through?

Yeah, I think so. Looking back, it was definitely there in grade school. I mean, I was always described as “bright,” which—funny, that word showed up on report cards a lot—but then right next to it would be things like “daydreams” or “needs to turn in work.”

And the weird thing is, sometimes I’d actually do the assignment and then just… not hand it in. Or I’d lose the homework folder. I can still picture those flimsy folders with the little metal tabs—anyway, that was happening way before I was a teenager. So yes, I don’t think this is new.
Have you ever had a period when you needed much less sleep than usual and still felt full of energy?

I’m not sure. I mean, I’ve had nights where I stayed up way too late because I got sucked into something, like reading or messing with a project, and then regretted it the next day. But “needed less sleep” and felt energized… I don’t think so? Not in any clear way.

I usually notice the opposite more, like if I don’t sleep enough I’m kind of dragging. Although there were times in school where I’d pull late nights and convince myself I was fine, but that might’ve just been caffeine and the deadline panic, not actual energy.
Do you often make careless mistakes because your attention slips, even when you know the material or task well?

Yeah, that happens. It’s frustrating because it’s not like I don’t understand the code or the task. In code reviews I’ll miss something embarrassingly small, like a condition that’s reversed, or a version number in a dependency file that’s clearly wrong, and then later when someone points it out I’m like—how did I not see that? It was right there.

And I think part of it is I’ll be skimming, sort of assuming the shape of the thing is correct because I’ve seen a hundred files like it before. Which is funny, not funny, but I’ll notice some weird architectural issue and then miss the tiny obvious thing sitting two lines above it.
In conversations, do you often realize you weren’t really listening even when someone is speaking directly to you?

Yeah. That happens more than I like to admit. In architecture meetings especially, someone will be talking right to me, and I’ll catch the first few words, but then my brain goes off on some implementation detail—like, “Wait, how would that service actually handle retries?”—and then suddenly they’re asking me a question.

And I’m sitting there realizing I don’t actually know what the last part was. So I have to say, “Sorry, can you repeat that?” which is awkward, because technically I was looking at them. I just wasn’t really… listening the whole time.
Do these attention and organization problems cause real difficulties in more than one part of your life, such as both at work and at home?

Yeah… I think so. Work is the clearest place, honestly. It’s gotten past just “I’m a little scattered” and into people noticing in ways that actually matter.

Like, I missed a checkpoint for a patent filing, which is not the kind of thing you can just shrug off. There are calendars and reminders and, you know, supposedly “process” around that stuff, but I still managed to let it slip. And then there was this architecture review that was already difficult—lots of moving pieces, different teams, everyone with opinions—and I didn’t keep it organized well enough. After that, I could tell some collaborators were questioning whether I should be leading the larger project.

At home it’s… I mean, yes, things spill over there too, but the work stuff is what really scared me, because reputation takes forever to build and apparently not that long to dent.
Do you often spend so much time trying to get things exactly right that it makes it hard to finish tasks?

I’m not sure that’s the main issue for me. I mean, I can get picky about things—especially with code, because one tiny thing can break something—but I don’t know that I’m usually stuck trying to make it perfect.

Sometimes I’ll spend too long tweaking something, but then again in software that can be hard to separate from just… doing the job properly. Like, you think you’re cleaning up one function and suddenly you’re wondering why the whole module is named wrong, and then you’ve lost the thread.

But if you mean perfectionism to the point where I can’t finish, I don’t really know. I haven’t noticed that as much as other problems.
Do you often find yourself worrying a lot about many different things?

I don’t know… I mean, I worry about things, sure, but “many different things” is hard to say.

Sometimes I think what looks like worry is more like my brain trying to run ten simulations at once, like if this happens then that happens, and then I remember some random thing from three weeks ago—actually, this happened with a home repair thing where I was looking up one part and ended up reading about electrical code for an hour, which was not even relevant.

But, sorry, the question was whether I worry a lot. I’m not sure I’d describe it that way exactly. I haven’t really thought of myself as a constant worrier.
Did these problems start after a specific stressful event in your life?

No, I don’t think it started after one specific stressful event. Looking back, it was there really early.

I remember—well, I don’t remember all of it directly, but my parents kept some old report cards, and teachers would write things like I was bright but daydreamed a lot, or I didn’t turn in work even when I’d done it. I had these homework folders that would just disappear, which is funny now except it wasn’t funny then, because everyone would act like I was being careless on purpose.

So… yeah, long before I was a teenager, definitely grade school. It just kind of followed me, I guess.
When you start worrying about something, do you usually find it hard to stop or control the worrying?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, sometimes a thought keeps looping, but I don’t know if I’d call it “worrying” exactly, or if it’s more like I’m trying to solve something in my head.

Like if there’s some issue with the house or work, I might keep coming back to it, and then I’ll look up one thing and end up down some completely different path. But whether I can’t control worry… I don’t know. I haven’t really tracked it that way. It’s not like I’m sitting there thinking, “I can’t stop worrying,” most of the time.
Do you often feel physically restless, like it’s hard to sit still?

Yeah, especially if I’m stuck on a long design call. I’ll be sitting there trying to look like I’m paying attention, and it’s like this pressure builds up in my body that I need to move.

So I’ll get up and pace around my office, or I’ll switch chairs, or kind of shift around a lot. It’s worse on calls where everyone is talking through architecture diagrams for, like, an hour—sorry, that’s probably too specific—but yeah, sitting still can be hard in those situations.
Do you often interrupt people or blurt things out before they’ve finished speaking?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I know I can get excited in conversations and jump in, especially if I think I understand where someone is going, but I don’t know if people would say I’m interrupting a lot.

Actually, it depends who I’m talking to—like at work, some meetings are kind of overlapping anyway, everyone talks over each other a bit, especially engineers when they’re debating some tiny implementation detail that turns into a whole thing about naming conventions… Sorry, I’m getting off track.

I guess I haven’t really noticed it as a major complaint. My wife might have a better answer than me on that.
Do you often fidget with your hands or feet when you’re supposed to stay seated?

Yeah, I think so. Not always like tapping my foot nonstop, but when I’m supposed to stay seated—especially on long design calls—I get this sort of pressure building up, like my body wants to get up even if I’m trying to look focused.

I’ll shift around in the chair a lot, or move to a different chair, and sometimes I just start pacing around my office while still listening. Which is probably fine because I’m at home most of the time, but if the camera’s on I’m trying to make it look like I’m still, you know, engaged.
Do you often feel tense or keyed up, even when nothing specific is happening?

Yeah, kind of. I don’t know if I’d call it “tense” exactly, but I do get this keyed-up feeling in my body, especially on those long design calls.

Like, I’ll be trying to sit there and look focused, and meanwhile there’s this pressure building like I need to get up. So I’ll start shifting around, or I’ll move from one chair to another, or just pace around my office while I’m listening. It’s funny because sometimes the call itself isn’t even stressful, it’s just… sitting there that long makes me feel like I need to move.
When you feel keyed up, is it usually because you’re worrying about something?

I’m not totally sure. Sometimes it probably is, but I don’t always have a specific worry attached to it.

Like, I can be sitting there and my body feels keyed up, but if you asked me what I’m anxious about, I might not have an answer. It’s more like… restlessness, maybe? Although then I start thinking about whether I forgot to reply to someone, or if there’s some message sitting in Slack—sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

So, I guess no, not usually because of one clear worry. Or at least I haven’t noticed it that way.
